Executive summary This case study describes an interactive Streamlit app for exploring tweets about airlines, grouped by positive, negative and neutral sentiment. Users can inspect sentiment distributions, filter by time and location, compare airlines and explore frequently used terms.
The project focuses on exploratory analysis and visualization of sentiment-labeled tweets. The original article does not document training or evaluating a new sentiment classification model. Its use of a tweet dataset should not be confused with verified real-time social media ingestion.
CASE STUDY Airline Sentiment Explorer — Streamlit Domain / DomínioData Analytics / Sentiment AnalysisTech StackPython · Streamlit · Pandas · ChartsFocus / FocoExploratory analysis · Filtering · Visual communicationDeliverables / EntregáveisInteractive app · Charts · Map · Word cloudStatusPortfolio application GitHub · Source Code / Código-fonte ↗
Problem and requirements Airline-related social media data contains varied opinions. Reading posts individually makes it difficult to compare perceptions across companies, dates and locations.
The application aims to:
explore tweets by sentiment category (positive, negative or neutral); compare distributions using bar charts and pie charts; filter activity over a selected time period; visualize geographic distribution on a map; compare sentiment across different airlines; summarize recurring terms through a word cloud. Architecture and data flow Tweet dataset with sentiment information │ ▼ Data selection / filtering │ ▼ Streamlit interface ┌────────┼─────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Sentiment Timeline & Airline comparison charts map and word cloud Input. A collection of tweets and their associated sentiment labels and supporting fields.
Processing. The app filters the data according to user selections and aggregates observations for display.
Output. Interactive visualizations intended to help users explore customer sentiment patterns.
This is a logical overview derived from the documented application features, not an assertion about an undocumented data ingestion or model-training pipeline.
Implementation decisions 1. Streamlit interface. A Python-first framework makes exploratory data views accessible through interactive components.
2. Multiple visual encodings. Bar and pie charts support different ways to inspect sentiment proportions. The word cloud provides a complementary, qualitative overview of frequent terms.
3. Time, location and airline comparisons. These filters let readers ask more focused questions than a global sentiment count alone.
4. Distinguishing data labels from model predictions. The original article does not establish how sentiment labels were generated, so this study does not claim supervised model training.
Demo The video below, originally recorded in Portuguese, shows the application:
The original project also provides a Streamlit app link. Availability of the hosted service may change.
Testing and data quality The following are recommended checks, not a statement that automated tests have already been implemented:
inspect missing and duplicate tweet records; validate supported sentiment labels and filter values; compare plotted counts with source aggregations; check whether time and country fields are parsed consistently; test empty filter results and missing geographic information; verify that the Streamlit charts remain usable on smaller screens. If model training is added in a future version, separate evaluation metrics and dataset leakage checks will be needed.
Results and limitations Demonstrated outcome: a Streamlit application with sentiment distributions, airline comparisons, temporal/geographic exploration and a word cloud.
Limitations: no verified classification accuracy, latency measurements, production monitoring or live-streaming pipeline is established by the available article. The current case study should be read as interactive analytics.
Lessons learned and next steps The project illustrates how interface design and filtering can make an analytical dataset easier to explore. A future technical iteration could add data-quality checks, explicit data lineage and, if appropriate, a separately documented sentiment classifier with proper train/test evaluation.

Executive summary This project explores a Power BI dashboard for sales and product returns at a fictional electronics retail chain. The solution transforms XLSX source files with Power Query and organizes three complementary analytical views: overall performance, product and brand performance, and returns.
The objective is to make business indicators easier to explore and support discussions about commercial performance and operational improvements. The project is a portfolio case study; it does not report production adoption or independently measured savings.
CASE STUDY Sales & Returns Analytics — Power BI Domain / DomínioData Analytics / Business IntelligenceTech StackPower BI · Power Query · XLSXFocus / FocoData preparation · KPI reporting · Interactive analysisDeliverables / EntregáveisInteractive dashboard · Sales, product and returns viewsStatusPortfolio case study (fictional business) Problem and requirements Sales, profitability and returned products are closely related, but reviewing these dimensions separately makes it difficult to understand what is happening in a store network. The fictional retail scenario calls for a reusable analytical view that can be explored by business users.
The dashboard should:
consolidate sales and returns inputs from XLSX files; organize the source data for consistent reporting; provide an overview of revenue, profit and sales; allow analysis by product, brand, period and geographic area; surface return patterns for investigation. Architecture and data flow XLSX source files │ ▼ Power Query — extraction, cleanup and normalization │ ▼ Prepared analytical dataset / data model │ ▼ Power BI dashboard ├── Overall performance: sales, revenue and profit ├── Product & brand: period and location filters └── Returns: distribution and recurring patterns Inputs. Sales and returns records are stored as spreadsheets.
Processing. Power Query applies extraction, cleaning and normalization to prepare data for dashboard analysis.
Consumption. Power BI provides interactive views intended for sales and management users.
Implementation decisions 1. Three business perspectives. The dashboard separates the global view from product/brand detail and returns. This helps readers navigate from a high-level indicator to a specific business question.
2. Interactive filters. Period and location filters make comparisons more useful than static exports.
3. Data preparation before visualization. Cleaning and normalizing input files in Power Query reduces ambiguity when the dashboard is refreshed from the prepared sources.
The original write-up describes the analytical views but does not document detailed DAX measures, a star schema or refresh infrastructure. Those details should only be added after reviewing the .pbix implementation.
Demo The original demonstration is in Portuguese and walks through the implemented dashboard:
Testing and data quality The following are recommended validation checks, not a claim that a formal automated test suite was implemented:
reconcile total sales and returns against the source spreadsheets; verify number, date and currency fields after import; check whether filters interact correctly across the three views; test duplicate, missing and inconsistent product identifiers; validate the meaning of profit and return indicators before comparing them; inspect dashboard usability at common screen sizes. Results and limitations Demonstrated deliverable: an interactive dashboard with views for overall performance, product/brand analysis and returns, based on a fictional retail scenario.
Limitations: no independently documented business impact, verified savings, deployment SLA or refresh benchmark. The work illustrates an analytical workflow, rather than a measured operational rollout.
Lessons learned and next steps The project demonstrates the value of structuring the data before presenting KPIs. A future revision could document the semantic model, DAX definitions and reproducible validation rules, then compare dashboard calculations against reference queries.
Repository and references The available artifact is the Power BI dashboard demonstration video. No source repository was linked in the original article.
Cover illustration credit: gstudioimagen / Freepik.

Executive summary Boutique Manager is a shell scripting project for a small clothing shop scenario. Its command-line menu brings together product registration, inventory updates, sales, stock alerts, reporting, logging and backups.
The project originated from applying concepts studied in the Hands-on Introduction to Linux Commands and Shell Scripting course. It is a practical automation exercise, rather than a claim of deployment at a commercial retailer.
CASE STUDY Boutique Manager — Bash Automation Domain / DomínioAutomation / Systems ScriptingTech StackBash · Linux · awk · sort · uniq · CronFocus / FocoInventory · Sales · File operations · AuditabilityDeliverables / EntregáveisTerminal menu · Sales reports · Logs · Scheduled backupsStatusDemonstration project GitHub · Source Code / Código-fonte ↗
Problem and requirements A small retailer needs a consistent way to track products and stock, record sales, and avoid losing operational data. Repeating manual file updates can introduce inconsistencies and is difficult to audit.
The command-line solution aims to:
register products and organize inventory by category; record sales with date, time and amounts; update stock after transactions, checking quantities before a sale; highlight low stock and report performance by category and period; keep operational logs and schedule backups; provide a simple menu for these operations. Architecture and data flow Command-line menu (Bash) │ ├── Product registry ───► Inventory files ├── Sales workflow ────► Stock updates + sales records ├── Reports ───────────► Aggregations by period/category └── Operations ────────► Timestamped logs │ Cron schedules ──────────────────────► Backups / stock checks Input. User selections and product/sales details entered in the terminal.
Processing. Shell functions manipulate structured files, validate stock quantities and prepare summaries.
Output. Updated inventory/sales records, reports, audit-style logs and backup artifacts.
Architecture illustration Tip: open the diagram in a separate browser tab to zoom in.
Implementation decisions 1. Bash modules and control flow. The project uses functions, parameters, if/then/else, case, while and iteration over categories to keep the interactive menu maintainable.
2. Text processing tools. Pipes and command-line filters such as awk, sort and uniq support report generation and aggregation of inventory and sales information.
3. Environment configuration and I/O. Variables including LOJA_DIR and DATA, export, file patterns, command substitution and redirection organize execution paths and logs.
4. Data integrity and auditability. The implementation describes quantity checks before sales, temporary-file updates and timestamped operation logs.
5. Scheduled operations. Cron is used to schedule recurring backups and inventory checks. The original article describes daily backups and weekly inventory checks.
Demo The project provides a visual architecture diagram above and a source repository.
Testing and data quality The following are recommended tests; a formal automated test suite was not documented:
prevent sales when requested quantity exceeds available inventory; validate product registration with missing or invalid fields; check whether inventory changes are consistent with sales records; verify report totals with a small known dataset; test recovery when temporary-file writes fail; ensure log timestamps are present and meaningful; check Cron jobs and restoration from generated backups. Results and limitations Demonstrated deliverable: a Bash-based management workflow for the described store scenario, combining sales, inventory, reports, logging and backups.
Limitations: there are no documented production users, measured time savings, concurrency guarantees or verified backup-restore benchmarks. Shell/file-based state management would require further hardening for multiple simultaneous users.
Lessons learned and next steps The case study shows how small shell utilities can be combined into a useful workflow. Future improvements could introduce shell linting (shellcheck), automated tests, explicit configuration management and a documented restore procedure for backups.

Executive summary This project demonstrates a straightforward Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) workflow written in Python. It consolidates records stored in CSV, JSON and XML files into a consistent dataset and produces two artifacts: transformed_data.csv and log_file.txt.
The case study focuses on the core engineering considerations behind the implementation: heterogeneous inputs, standardization rules, repeatable execution and traceability through logs. It is a small-scale educational pipeline, rather than a production platform.
CASE STUDY Python ETL — Unified Data Pipeline Domain / DomínioData EngineeringTech StackPython · pandas · glob · ElementTree · datetimeFocus / FocoExtraction · standardization · loggingDeliverables / Entregáveistransformed_data.csv · log_file.txtStatusDemonstration project GitHub · Source Code / Código-fonte ↗
Problem and requirements Operational data frequently arrives from several systems and in different file formats. Even when files contain similar fields, ingesting each source separately increases manual work and the risk of inconsistent transformations.
For this example, records contain name, height and weight fields. The goal is to read the available files, harmonize their structure and measurement units, and write a single CSV suitable for subsequent analysis or database ingestion.
The workflow should:
read files in CSV, JSON and XML formats; combine compatible records in a standardized tabular structure; apply explicit transformation rules to measurement units; save a unified dataset and record execution events in a log file. Architecture and data flow CSV files ─┐ JSON files ├──► EXTRACT ──► TRANSFORM ──► LOAD ──► transformed_data.csv XML files ─┘ │ │ │ └─────────────┴──────────┴──► log_file.txt Extract. Python discovers and reads source files. pandas handles tabular data and ElementTree can parse XML records.
Transform. Records are combined into a consistent table. The example includes conversion of height from inches to meters and weight from pounds to kilograms, according to the source units. Verify that each input uses those units before applying a conversion.
Load. The transformed dataset is written to transformed_data.csv, while log_file.txt records execution events and supports troubleshooting.
Implementation choices The project uses widely available Python tools rather than adding unnecessary infrastructure:
Component Role glob Discover files matching expected patterns pandas Combine and transform structured records xml.etree.ElementTree Read XML input datetime Add timestamps to execution logs CSV output Create a reusable dataset The main design trade-off is simplicity versus extensibility. This solution fits a controlled set of sample input files; it would need stronger schemas, error handling and orchestration for a production workload.
Demo The original walkthrough is available below (video in Portuguese):
Validation and testing For a reliable ETL pipeline, quality checks should cover more than whether an output file exists. The following is a recommended validation checklist, not a claim that an automated test suite has already been implemented:
Confirm that CSV, JSON and XML readers return the expected fields. Check that records have consistent field types after transformation. Validate unit conversions with known examples (e.g., 70 inches = 1.778 meters; 150 pounds ≈ 68.04 kg). Compare input and output record counts, accounting for intentional exclusions. Check behavior for empty files, missing columns and invalid values. Confirm that the log records start, completion and failure events. A future iteration could add pytest, schema validation and CI checks before publishing new outputs.
Results and limitations The described implementation produces a unified CSV file and an execution log, reducing the need to manually open each source format before analysis. No runtime benchmark, throughput measurement or percentage reduction in effort has been reported for this demonstration.
Key limitations include limited input schemas, absence of a documented automated test suite and no orchestration or monitoring layer. These are opportunities for future development, not capabilities already demonstrated.
Lessons learned and next steps Even small ETL tasks benefit from clear transformation rules, auditable outputs and reproducible processing. A natural progression toward production-grade Data Engineering would be to add automated testing, configuration management, structured logging and scheduled execution.
